claims.text: The starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a coarse-grained, single-phase solid-solution state.
Grain size and associated grain-boundary density govern the hardness, strength, and deformation behavior of nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The coarse-grained solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity predominates in coarse-grained CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid quenching followed by controlled annealing or severe plastic deformation can produce nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi.
Grain refinement increases the volume fraction or density of grain boundaries.
The additional grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary strengthening reinforces solid-solution hardening in refined CoCrFeNiTi.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi will have higher hardness than its coarse-grained counterpart.
Nanocrystalline CoCrFeNiTi will have higher compressive strength than its coarse-grained counterpart.
Refinement to the nanocrystalline regime causes a transition from dislocation-glide-dominated deformation to grain-boundary-mediated deformation.
The predicted increases in hardness and compressive strength will be accompanied by reduced plastic strain or ductility.
The proposed controlled comparison uses coarse-grained and nanocrystalline samples of the same equimolar CoCrFeNiTi composition tested under identical room-temperature conditions.
The hypothesis is limited to room-temperature tests at moderate strain rates typical of nanoindentation and compression.
Behavior at elevated temperature or high strain rate may differ because of additional thermally activated processes such as grain-boundary sliding.
The magnitudes of the predicted property changes in CoCrFeNiTi are unknown.
Minor secondary phases or segregation may confound the proposed grain-size effect.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in both hardness and compressive strength, together with decreased ductility, in the nanocrystalline sample would falsify the hypothesis.
